definition.text: The elasticity of substitution measures how easily one input or good can be swapped for another: the percentage change in their ratio of use for a percentage change in their relative marginal values or prices.

facts.text: Its most common use is the ratio of capital to labour relative to the ratio of their marginal products or prices.
John Hicks introduced it in 1932, and Joan Robinson independently discovered it in 1933.
It measures the curvature of an isoquant; the larger it is, the more readily one input is substituted for another.
Below one, goods are gross complements and relative spending on a good rises with its relative price; above one they are gross substitutes and it falls.
At exactly one, the Cobb–Douglas case, relative spending does not depend on relative prices.

definition.text: The overlapping generations (OLG) model is a leading framework in macroeconomic dynamics in which people live for a finite time, long enough to overlap with other generations.

facts.text: It is the natural framework for studying how resources are allocated across generations, for example through Social Security.
Maurice Allais first formulated it in 1947, Paul Samuelson more rigorously in 1958, and Peter Diamond added production in 1965.
Its steady-state equilibrium need not be efficient, unlike general equilibrium models covered by the first welfare theorem; in Diamond's version people save more than is socially optimal.
